hmmt-nov-2018-thm-01.title: Solution
hmmt-nov-2018-thm-01.body:
The pentagon's vertices divide the circle into $5$ arcs of $72^\circ$, and the four vertices of the square (spaced $90^\circ$ apart, with none at a pentagon vertex) lie in four different arcs. Hence each side of the square crosses exactly two sides of the pentagon, giving $4\cdot2=8$ intersections.

**Answer: 8**

hmmt-nov-2018-thm-02.title: Solution
hmmt-nov-2018-thm-02.body:
The sum $\overline{CASH}+\overline{ME}$ is less than $9999+99<11000$, so $O=1$ and the second digit $S=0$. Looking at the units digit, $H+E\equiv E\pmod{10}$ gives $H=0$. But then $\overline{CASH}+\overline{ME}\le9900+99<10000$, so it cannot be a $5$-digit number. No assignments work.

**Answer: 0**

hmmt-nov-2018-thm-03.title: Solution
hmmt-nov-2018-thm-03.body:
$H\ne B$ (otherwise $DAB$ would be equilateral and not collinear). Triangles $HOW$ and $BOW$ share the side $OW=7$ and are both equilateral, on opposite sides of $OW$, so $HB=7\sqrt3$ (the two apexes of a rhombus with side $7$ and angles $60^\circ,120^\circ$).

Let $M$ be the midpoint of $DA$; since $DAH$ is equilateral with side $2$, $HM\perp DA$ and $HM=\sqrt3$, $AM=1$. As $B$ lies on line $DA$, $\angle HMB=90^\circ$, so $BM=\sqrt{(7\sqrt3)^2-(\sqrt3)^2}=\sqrt{147-3}=12$. Therefore $BA=BM-AM=12-1=11$.

**Answer: 11**

hmmt-nov-2018-thm-04.title: Solution
hmmt-nov-2018-thm-04.body:
Suppose he buys $a$ packages of $7$ and $b$ of $12$ at first, and $c$ of $7$ and $d$ of $12$ later: $6a+10b=n$, $6c+10d=n+2$, $7a+12b>7c+12d$. The $12$-packs give more pencils per cent, so we need $b>d$. Subtracting the equations and halving: $3(c-a)-5(b-d)=1$, and the pencil inequality is $12(b-d)>7(c-a)$.

The solutions with $b-d>0$ are $(c-a,b-d)=(2,1),(7,4),(12,7),(17,10),\dots$ Checking $12(b-d)>7(c-a)$: $12>14$ no, $48>49$ no, $84>84$ no, $120>119$ yes. So $b-d\ge10$, hence $b\ge10$ and $n\ge100$. And $(a,b,c,d)=(0,10,17,0)$ gives $n=100$: $100$ cents buys $120$ pencils, $102$ cents buys $17$ packs of $7$ for $119$ pencils.

**Answer: 100**

hmmt-nov-2018-thm-05.title: Solution
hmmt-nov-2018-thm-05.body:
Let $p_n$ be the probability of rain $n$ days from today, $p_0=0$. Then $p_{n+1}=\frac34p_n+\frac14(1-p_n)=\frac14+\frac12p_n$, so $p_{n+1}-\frac12=\frac12\left(p_n-\frac12\right)$ and $p_n=\frac12-\frac1{2^{n+1}}$. We need $\frac1{2^{n+1}}<\frac1{1000}$, i.e. $2^{n+1}>1000$, first true for $n+1=10$, $n=9$.

**Answer: 9**

hmmt-nov-2018-thm-06.title: Solution
hmmt-nov-2018-thm-06.body:
Use the factorial base: every integer has a unique expansion $k=\sum_{i=1}^6d_i\,i!$ with $0\le d_i\le i$. The nice numbers are exactly those whose digits satisfy $1\le d_i\le i$ for all $i$ (so $d_1=1$), which also automatically respects the limit of $i$ copies of the $i$-coin.

Count nice $k<2018$ by the leading digit $d_6$ (digits $d_5,\dots,d_2$ free in $1..i$):
- $d_6=1$: $5\cdot4\cdot3\cdot2=120$ choices of $(d_5,d_4,d_3,d_2)$, and the largest such number is $720+600+96+18+4+1=1439<2018$. All count: $120$.
- $d_6=2$: the remainder $120d_5+24d_4+6d_3+2d_2+1$ must be at most $2017-1440=577$. $d_5\le3$: all of the $4\cdot3\cdot2=24$ lower choices work, giving $3\cdot24=72$. $d_5=4$: need $24d_4+6d_3+2d_2+1\le97$; this holds for $d_4\le3$ ($72+18+4+1=95$) and fails for $d_4=4$ ($96+6+2+1=105$): $3\cdot3\cdot2=18$. $d_5=5$ gives $600>577$. So $72+18=90$.
- $d_6\ge3$ gives numbers $\ge2160>2018$.

Total $120+90=210$.

**Answer: 210**

hmmt-nov-2018-thm-07.title: Solution
hmmt-nov-2018-thm-07.body:
Since $IE$ is the perpendicular bisector of $KT$, the diagonals of the kite are perpendicular and $R$ is the midpoint of $KT$. Let $[KIR]=[RIT]=a$ and $[KER]=[TER]=b$, so $[KITE]=2a+2b$.

$[RAIN]=[RAI]+[RIN]$. Since $A$ is the midpoint of $KI$, $[RAI]=\frac12[RKI]=\frac a2$; similarly $[RIN]=\frac a2$. So $a=[RAIN]=4$.

Now split $[MAKE]=[MAD]+[AKD]+[DEM]$ (using the point $D$ on $KE$). In the midpoint quadrilateral, $AD\parallel IE$ with $AD=\frac{IE}2$ and $DM\parallel KT$ with $DM=\frac{KT}2$, and $IE\perp KT$, so $[MAD]=\frac12\cdot\frac{IE}2\cdot\frac{KT}2=\frac{[KITE]}4=\frac{a+b}2$. Triangle $AKD$ is similar to $KIE$ with ratio $\frac12$, so $[AKD]=\frac{[KIE]}4=\frac{a+b}4$, and likewise $[DEM]=\frac{[KTE]}4=\frac b2$. Hence
$$[MAKE]=\frac{3a+5b}4=18\ \Rightarrow\ 3a+5b=72\ \Rightarrow\ b=12.$$
Finally $[DIME]=2[IME]=[ITE]=a+b=16$.

**Answer: 16**

hmmt-nov-2018-thm-08.title: Solution
hmmt-nov-2018-thm-08.body:
After $u$ jumps of $3$ and $v$ jumps of $7$ Crisp is at $3u+7v$. Modulo $5$ this is $3u+2v\equiv3(u-v)$, so he is on a multiple of $5$ exactly when $u-v\equiv0\pmod5$, and he stops the first time this happens. Modulo $2$ the position is $u+v\equiv u-v$, so he stops on a dime (even multiple of $5$) if $u-v=0$ and on a nickel if $u-v=\pm5$. So he stops on a dime iff the walk $n=u-v$ returns to $0$ before reaching $\pm5$.

*First jump is a $3$* ($n=1$, step $+1$ with probability $\frac23$, $-1$ with $\frac13$): the probability $a_i$ of reaching $0$ before $5$ from $i$ satisfies $a_1=\frac23a_2+\frac13$, $a_2=\frac23a_3+\frac13a_1$, $a_3=\frac23a_4+\frac13a_2$, $a_4=\frac13a_3$, giving $a_1=\frac{15}{31}$.

*First jump is a $7$* (let $m=v-u=1$; steps $+1$ with probability $\frac13$ and $-1$ with probability $\frac23$): $b_1=\frac13b_2+\frac23$, $b_2=\frac13b_3+\frac23b_1$, $b_3=\frac13b_4+\frac23b_2$, $b_4=\frac23b_3$, giving $b_1=\frac{30}{31}$.

The answer is $\frac23\cdot\frac{15}{31}+\frac13\cdot\frac{30}{31}=\frac{20}{31}$.

**Answer: $\frac{20}{31}$**

hmmt-nov-2018-thm-09.title: Solution
hmmt-nov-2018-thm-09.body:
Use complex numbers: the square's vertices are $1,i,-1,-i$ and the pentagon's vertices are $2\alpha\omega^k$ with $|\alpha|=1$, $\omega=e^{2\pi i/5}$. For a point $z$ the product of distances to the square's vertices is $|(z-1)(z-i)(z+1)(z+i)|=|z^4-1|$. So the total product is
$$\prod_{k=0}^{4}\left|16\alpha^4\omega^{4k}-1\right|=\left|\prod_{k}(16\alpha^4\omega^{k}-1)\right|=\left|(16\alpha^4)^5-1\right|=|2^{20}\alpha^{20}-1|,$$
(since $\omega^{4k}$ runs over all fifth roots of unity). By the triangle inequality this is at most $2^{20}+1$, with equality when $\alpha^{20}=-1$.

**Answer: $2^{20}+1=1048577$**

hmmt-nov-2018-thm-10.title: Solution
hmmt-nov-2018-thm-10.body:
An honest buck's statement is true, so he has at most one honest neighbor, hence at least $3$ dishonest neighbors. A dishonest buck's statement is false, so he has at least two honest neighbors. Let $K$ be the number of honest bucks and $B$ the number of buckaroo pairs (honest-dishonest neighbours). Counting from the honest side, $B\ge3K$; counting from the dishonest side, $B\ge2(10^6-K)$. Taking the weighted average $\frac25\cdot3K+\frac35\cdot2(10^6-K)$ of these two lower bounds, $B\ge\frac65\cdot10^6=1200000$.

Equality: colour the cell $(x,y)$ by $x+2y\bmod5$ (well defined on the torus since $5\mid1000$); each colour class has $200000$ cells. Make the bucks of colours $0$ and $1$ honest. A cell of colour $r$ has neighbours of colours $r\pm1,r\pm2$, i.e. all four other colours. So each honest buck has exactly one honest neighbour (the other honest colour) and each dishonest buck has exactly two honest neighbours: all statements are consistent, and $B=3\cdot400000=1200000$.

**Answer: 1200000**
